The word chink has three distinct meanings as a noun. You need to know all three to use and understand it correctly.
Meaning 1: A narrow crack or gap

This is the most common and important meaning.

A chink is a very small, narrow opening — a thin gap or crack — in something that is otherwise solid or closed. Think of it as a tiny slit that breaks through a surface.

Examples:

  • A wall made of old bricks might have a chink between two bricks where the cement has crumbled away.
  • If a door doesn't close perfectly and leaves a thin sliver of space, that sliver is a chink.
  • Boards on an old wooden fence often have chinks between them.

The key idea is narrowness. A chink is not a wide hole or a large break — it is always a thin, tight little gap.
Meaning 2: A narrow ray or beam of light passing through such a gap

This meaning grows naturally from Meaning 1 and they are often used together.

When light passes through a chink (a narrow crack), that thin sliver of light itself is also called a chink of light. It is the beam or streak of light that sneaks through a small opening.

Examples:

  • Early in the morning, a chink of light crept through the curtains and fell across the floor.
  • The room was completely dark except for a single chink of light coming through a gap in the shutters.
  • He peeked through a chink of light between the fence boards to see what was happening on the other side.

You will almost always see this meaning used as "a chink of light" — those three words tend to travel together.
Meaning 3: A short, light, ringing sound

A chink can also describe a small, sharp, metallic or glassy tinkling sound — the kind of sound produced when two hard, light objects tap against each other.

Examples:

  • She heard the chink of coins as he dropped them onto the table.
  • There was a soft chink of glasses as they touched them together in a toast.
  • The chink of keys in his pocket announced his arrival before he even opened the door.

Think of it as a brief, clean, high-pitched click or ring — lighter and shorter than a "clang" or a "clunk."
Meaning 4: A racial slur (important to know, never to use)

You must be aware of this meaning so you are never caught off guard when you encounter it, and so you never accidentally use the word in a context where it could be misunderstood.

Chink is also a deeply offensive and hurtful racial slur used against people of Chinese or, more broadly, East Asian descent. It is considered one of the most hateful anti-Asian terms in the English language.

You should never use it in this sense. It causes real harm and is widely regarded as unacceptable in all social, professional, and academic contexts.

When you see the word in literature, journalism, or everyday speech, context will almost always make it immediately clear which meaning is intended — a crack in a wall, a beam of light, a ringing sound, or the slur. Educated, respectful speakers and writers use meanings 1, 2, and 3 freely and naturally; meaning 4 is used only by people who intend to insult.

As a learner, here is how to remember chink:

  • Physical: A thin crack or gap in something solid.
  • Visual: The narrow ray of light that slips through that crack.
  • Auditory: A brief, delicate, ringing tap of hard objects.
  • Harmful: A slur — know it exists, never use it.

The first three meanings are entirely normal, everyday English words. You will encounter them regularly in novels, newspapers, and conversation, and you should feel confident using them yourself.
